title: Brendan the Navigator (16 May)
hookLine: an Irish monk whose ocean voyage became a legend

lines: A BOAT OF WOOD AND HIDES.
cards: A small boat of wood and hides, pushed off a rocky Irish shore. Monks at the oars, an abbot at the front, and no map for where they're going. They're looking for a land promised to the saints, somewhere out to the west.
Some days the wind takes them. Some days they row. Some days they simply pull in the oars and let God steer.
Then they land on a dark, bare island, light a fire to cook, and the island starts to move.

teach.b: There was a real Brendan, an Irish abbot who founded monasteries and is remembered as a traveler. And there's the Brendan of the Voyage, a Latin tale called the Navigatio.
The two overlap, but the Voyage is a legend, and it wears its wonders openly.

teach.h: EASTER ON THE BACK OF A WHALE.
teach.b: The moving island is a great fish; in the tale, the monks come back to it each Easter to keep the feast on its back. They find an island of birds that sing the hours of prayer.
They meet a monk who has lived alone on a rock. They sail past wonders and terrors.

Some readers have wondered whether a real voyage lies under the story, maybe even across the whole Atlantic, and people have argued about it. The tale itself doesn't care to prove anything. It's after something else.
Irish tradition speaks of leaving home for God's sake, with no plan to come back; some call it a kind of white martyrdom. Brendan's boat is that idea, set afloat.

teach.h: PRAYERS KEPT ON A TINY BOAT.
teach.b: The sea is huge and the boat is tiny, and the monks keep their prayers anyway, at their hours, even on the back of a whale.
There's a psalm about sailors, in the Douay-Rheims: "They that go down to the sea in ships, doing business in the great waters: These have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep."
That's the Voyage in two lines: the farther out the monks go, the more wonders they meet.

how: Saint Brendan's day is kept on 16 May, especially in Ireland; Catholics remember him with prayers for sailors and travelers, and some coastal communities bless boats.

games.q: you're one of Brendan's monks. you've lit a fire on a bare island, and the ground starts to move. what do you do?
games.why: the monks scramble back into the boat. the island is a great fish, and in the tale they return to it to keep Easter.

practice: Let your breath come and go like a slow swell, and bring to mind the people out on the water right now: fishing crews, sailors on cargo ships far from home for months, people crossing in boats that aren't safe, hoping to land somewhere, rescue crews heading into the weather.
If you pray, ask Saint Brendan to pray for them; if you don't, simply hold them, one boat at a time.

wordCard.voice: Navigatio, the Latin tale of Brendan the Navigator's legendary ocean voyage, carrying monks and their prayers far out to sea.

orig.note: Latin: a voyage, a sailing — the title of the tale of Brendan.
